title: What makes you valuable, when your skills are automated?
author: Elina
summary: Writing in The Silent Struggle, Elina argues that the old formula of choosing a profession, mastering its skills and receiving security and a title is losing its reliability as AI makes knowledge obsolete faster than people can absorb it. She proposes asking how to create value as a human rather than only as an expert, and offers four capabilities to build: sense-making, vision-setting, emotional awareness with cognitive flexibility, and social connection. For each she gives checklists for recognizing when it is a strength and when it needs work, and she cites research on AI-assisted writing and AI companionship to show the limits of outsourcing synthesis and connection. Underneath all four she places self-authorship, the ability to define your own value and direction. She stresses that this adds a layer to technical expertise rather than rejecting AI or learning skills.
points: As knowledge-based skills are automated, the useful question shifts from which skill to learn next to how an individual creates value as a human.
Capabilities such as sense-making and vision-setting are built through practice and show up as your own way of dealing with reality, which makes them hard to automate.
Sense-making is a judgement skill that atrophies when synthesis is outsourced, as the cited study of AI-assisted writing and weaker recall suggests.
The research on AI companionship is mixed: it can ease loneliness in the moment, but only human conversation produced lasting improvement in the trial she cites.
Self-authorship, defining your own worth and direction without outside confirmation, underlies all four capabilities and can be built deliberately.
quotes: The way we think is set early, shaped by the values and beliefs formed in our early years, and that’s not a great design for a world where the pace of change keeps accelerating.
What does look increasingly certain is that AI can make knowledge obsolete faster than we can absorb it.
Sense-making was never about finding the one correct interpretation. It’s building a good enough read of a messy situation, so you can move forward and keep revising it as you go.
When we outsource the synthesis, we stop building the connections that make judgement possible later. Use it or lose it applies here as much as anywhere.
you can hold two conflicting reads of a person or event without rushing to resolve it
AI can convincingly simulate being heard in the moment, but it has no stake in you, no friction of its own, nothing that builds the kind of durable trust real relationships require.
Building nurturing social connections is probably the most important capability we need to nurture, not only for leadership, but for the sake of our own well-being.

This is not a call to reject AI or learning technical skills. This is a call to augment our expertise with a new layer, that might sound less concrete, but could in fact create the winning combination, shaping your unique value.
